Explicit Instructions

  1. 1Look at the source carefully. Each card begins with a real photograph, poster or speech from the 1930s, and its details matter more than the first impression it gives.
  2. 2Read the claim and the three statements. Someone has used the source to make a claim, and your task is to choose the statement that the source can actually support.
  3. 3A wrong choice is crossed out. You can simply try again, because there are no points, no timer and no penalty.
  4. 4Read the explanation. It shows how a source like this can mislead, and you may open “What historians add” for further context.
  5. 5There are ten cards in three groups. Four come from Nazi Germany, three from the Soviet Union and three from Fascist Italy.

Questions to ask of any source

  1. What do I actually see here, and what am I being made to believe?
  2. Who made it, for whom, and what did they want people to think?
  3. What other evidence would I need before I believe the bigger claim?
A word of caution

Propaganda and manipulation did not end with the regimes of the 1930s; they are very much alive today. Social media and AI-generated images, text and video now make it easier than ever to produce material that looks convincing and spreads quickly. Asking what a source can actually prove has therefore become more important, not less, and it is a habit worth practising for your own sake.
